title: The Indian Premier League (IPL) is the world’s most valuable cricket
text:
###————————————————————————–### ### CONTEXT NOTE FOR READER ### ### Why the IPL Matters — For Non-Cricket Audiences ### ###————————————————————————–###

The Indian Premier League (IPL) is the world’s most valuable cricket


franchise tournament, generating over USD 15 billion in brand value


(Duff & Phelps, 2023) and attracting the highest-paid cricketers globally.


Established in 2008 by the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI),


it operates as a Twenty20 (T20) league — the shortest and most commercially


dominant format of the sport, where each team faces exactly 20 overs


(120 legal deliveries) per innings.


WHY IT MATTERS GLOBALLY:


─────────────────────────


1. SCALE: The IPL is the second most-attended sporting league in the world


by average attendance per game, behind only the NFL (ESPN, 2023).


The 2023 IPL final alone drew 130 million television viewers in India.


2. FINANCIAL DOMINANCE: Media rights for the 2023–2027 cycle were sold


for USD 6.2 billion — surpassing the per-match value of the English


Premier League. Every major cricket board now models its domestic


T20 league on the IPL structure.


3. TALENT CONCENTRATION: All 10 IPL franchises actively recruit from


every cricket-playing nation. Players from Australia (BBL), Pakistan


(PSL), West Indies (CPL), South Africa (SA20) and England (The Hundred)


compete in the IPL — making it the de facto global standard-setter


for T20 cricket strategy, rules, and innovation.


4. RULE-MAKING POWER: Because of its financial and cultural dominance,


what the BCCI does in the IPL influences cricket globally. When the


IPL introduced the Impact Player rule in 2023, other leagues immediately


began debating whether to adopt it. The ICC (International Cricket


Council) is watching closely.


WHY THE IMPACT PLAYER RULE IS A GLOBAL POLICY QUESTION:


─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────


The Impact Player rule allows teams to substitute one player mid-match


for tactical — not injury — reasons. A team may replace a struggling


batter with a specialist, or bring in an extra bowler after assessing


match conditions. This is unprecedented in cricket’s history and


structurally analogous to the designated hitter rule in MLB — a


substitution mechanic that fundamentally altered team composition,


player valuation, and strategic approach.


Unlike baseball’s DH rule which took decades to be universally adopted,


the IPL’s global reach means the Impact Player rule could reshape


cricket’s player development pipeline — specifically the value placed


on all-rounders (players who both bat and bowl at a high level) —


within a single generation of players.


The BCCI’s post-IPL 2026 review therefore carries implications not just


for Indian domestic cricket but for how the next generation of cricketers


worldwide are identified, developed, and valued at auction.


WHAT THIS PAPER CONTRIBUTES:


──────────────────────────────


This is the first causal analysis of the Impact Player rule using


ball-by-ball data across four T20 leagues (IPL, BBL, PSL, CPL) and


four outcome dimensions (run rate, wicket-taking, competitive balance,


all-rounder deployment). The timing is deliberate — the BCCI review


begins immediately after IPL 2026 concludes, and this paper provides


the empirical evidence base that policy discussion currently lacks.
###————————————————————————–##

title: Benching the All-Rounder: A Causal Analysis of the IPL Impact Player Rule
text:
Replication code available at: https://github.com/KeziahVickraman/ipl-impact-player
The Indian Premier League (IPL) introduced the Impact Player rule in 2023, allowing teams to substitute a specialist player mid-match for tactical purposes— the first such substitution mechanic in professional cricket’s history. Using ball-by-ball data from over 288,000 deliveries across IPL seasons 2008–2026, we employ Difference-in-Differences (DiD) and Synthetic Control methods to estimate the causal effect of this rule on four outcomes: run rates, wicket-taking rates, competitive balance, and all-rounder deployment. We find that the rule caused a significant increase in run rates of +1.3 runs per over and a significant decline in all-rounder deployment of −1.2 players per match. Synthetic control analysis confirms these effects cannot be attributed to global T20 trends— donor leagues BBL, PSL, and CPL show no comparable shifts. Analysis of lower-order batting patterns further reveals that position 8 strike rates increased by 16 points post-rule while bowling contribution fell by 9.5 percentage points, empirically validating practitioner concerns about the systematic displacement of the all-rounder archetype. With the BCCI announcing a formal review of the rule following IPL 2026, this paper provides the first rigorous causal evidence base to inform that decision.

title: Benching the All-Rounder: A Causal Analysis of the IPL Impact Player Rule
text:
2.1 The IPL and T20 Cricket
The Indian Premier League is the world’s most valuable cricket franchise tournament, generating over USD 15 billion in brand value and attracting the highest-paid cricketers globally. Established in 2008 by the BCCI, it operates as a Twenty20 (T20) league— the shortest and most commercially dominant format, where each team faces exactly 20 overs (120 legal deliveries) per innings.
The Impact Player rule introduced in 2023 remains unique to the IPL as of the 2026 season— the Big Bash League (BBL), Pakistan Super League (PSL), and Caribbean Premier League (CPL) have not adopted it or any structural equivalent. This is precisely what makes these leagues valid control units for our causal analysis.

title: Benching the All-Rounder: A Causal Analysis of the IPL Impact Player Rule
text:
2.2 The Impact Player Rule
Prior to 2023, cricket’s substitution rules were limited to injury replacements who could not bat or bowl. From IPL 2023, each team may name five potential Impact Players before the toss, then substitute one into the playing eleven at any point. The substituted player may bat or bowl. Franchises have overwhelmingly deployed it as a batting substitution— bringing in a specialist batter to accelerate a chase.
Former Indian international Sanjay Manjrekar identified the structural consequence:

“In Indian conditions, an Impact Sub batter has a far greater impact than an Impact Sub bowler… we are seeing pure batters like Ashutosh Sharma playing at number 8.”— Sportstar Insight Edge Podcast (2026)

This mechanism is particularly acute in Indian conditions— flat, dry pitches with minimal lateral movement mean an extra batter is almost always more valuable than an extra bowler. Crucially, this has an implication for our synthetic control: donor leagues operate in conditions where bowling Impact Players would be more viable, so our counterfactual represents a conservative lower bound on the true batting bias in Indian conditions.

title: Benching the All-Rounder: A Causal Analysis of the IPL Impact Player Rule
text:
4.1 Difference-in-Differences
Our first identification strategy compares IPL outcomes before and after 2023 against donor leagues that never adopted the rule. The estimating equation is:
\[Y_{lt} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Post}_t + \beta_2 \text{Treated}_l + \beta_3 (\text{Post}_t \times \text{Treated}_l) + \varepsilon_{lt}\]
where \(\beta_3\) — the interaction term— is the DiD estimate, equal to \((B-A) - (D-C)\) in the standard four-quadrant framework.

title: Benching the All-Rounder: A Causal Analysis of the IPL Impact Player Rule
text:
4.2 Synthetic Control
A limitation of DiD is the parallel trends assumption. As we show below, this assumption is not strictly satisfied in the pre-period. We therefore employ Synthetic Control (Abadie et al. 2010), which constructs a weighted combination of donor leagues to match IPL’s pre-treatment trajectory, then projects this counterfactual forward. The gap between actual and synthetic IPL is the estimated treatment effect.

section: 5.3 Parallel Trends and the Case for Synthetic Control
text:
5.3 Parallel Trends and the Case for Synthetic Control








Figure 3: Run rate trends, IPL versus donor leagues. Pre-2023 trends do not strictly satisfy the parallel trends assumption, motivating the use of Synthetic Control.





Because the parallel trends assumption is not strictly satisfied, we proceed to Synthetic Control, which relaxes this assumption by constructing a data-driven counterfactual rather than assuming common trends.

title: Benching the All-Rounder: A Causal Analysis of the IPL Impact Player Rule
text:
5.4 Synthetic Control Estimates








Figure 4: Synthetic Control: actual versus counterfactual IPL run rate. Post-2023, actual IPL run rates exceed the synthetic counterfactual constructed from donor leagues.













Figure 5: Synthetic Control: actual versus counterfactual all-rounder usage. Without the rule, all-rounder deployment would have risen; instead it falls— the lines move in opposite directions.





The synthetic control confirms the all-rounder finding is not attributable to global T20 trends. Without the rule, all-rounder deployment would have risen in line with donor leagues; instead it falls sharply— the actual and counterfactual trajectories move in opposite directions post-2023.

title: Benching the All-Rounder: A Causal Analysis of the IPL Impact Player Rule
section: 5.5 Specialist Displacement: Validating the Manjrekar Hypothesis
text:
5.5 Specialist Displacement: Validating the Manjrekar Hypothesis








Figure 6: Lower-order strike rates, pre versus post. Position 8 batters strike 16 points higher post-rule, consistent with pure batters replacing all-rounders.













Figure 7: Share of lower-order batters who also bowled, pre versus post. All-rounder deployment at positions 7-9 declined across the board post-2023.





These two figures provide the mechanism behind the aggregate all-rounder decline. Post-rule, position 8 batters strike 16 points higher while bowling 9.5 percentage points less— empirical confirmation that the Impact Player rule has systematically replaced the all-rounder archetype with pure batting specialists, exactly as Manjrekar observed.

title: Benching the All-Rounder: A Causal Analysis of the IPL Impact Player Rule
text:
6.1 The Indian Conditions Amplifier
Our synthetic control donor leagues— BBL, PSL, and CPL— operate in conditions where bowling Impact Players are more viable than in India. Australian pitches offer pace and bounce; Pakistani and Caribbean surfaces provide more lateral movement than the flat, dry tracks typical of the IPL. This means our counterfactual is conservative: the true batting bias introduced by the rule in Indian conditions is likely larger than our estimates suggest. Manjrekar’s observation is not anecdotal— it is empirically supported by the asymmetry our data reveals.

title: Benching the All-Rounder: A Causal Analysis of the IPL Impact Player Rule
text:
6.2 Policy Implications for the BCCI
The BCCI faces three options in its post-2026 review:

Keep the rule. Entertainment value is demonstrably higher. But all-rounder deployment continues to decline each season with no sign of reverting.
Modify the rule. Restricting the Impact Player to a like-for-like substitution, or to bowling substitutions only, could preserve excitement while protecting all-rounder value.
Scrap the rule. This would reverse the structural decline in all-rounder development but sacrifice the scoring gains that have driven viewership.

Our analysis cannot make this decision for the BCCI— but it provides the empirical evidence base that the discussion currently lacks.
